paragraphs: Multiple machine tool setters, operators, and tenders (O*NET-SOC 51-4081.00) set up, operate, or tend more than one cutting or forming machine tool or robot according to process documents and drawings, delivering metal or plastic parts that meet dimensional and appearance requirements. Their work involves compliant workholding, parameter setup, dimensional inspection, and traceable records of each batch's machining status.

If you willingly check drawings and process sheets item by item, understand dimensional tolerances and surface requirements, and remain alert to abnormal sounds, vibration, temperatures, and alarms while multiple machines run, these are more useful positive signals than simply liking machines.

Caution signals include skipping first-piece inspection or measuring instrument calibration to meet production targets, changing parameters from experience without checking process documents, or bypassing safety interlocks to continue operating after alarms. These issues directly create batch scrap, equipment damage, or personal injury.

Start with a paper process walkthrough: Using an entirely fictional drawing and process sheet, describe workholding, tool or die selection, critical dimensions and measuring instruments, first-piece inspection items, batch sampling frequency, and three safety confirmation points. Explain the response sequence when dimensions are out of tolerance. Use only fictional or public sample drawings and do not operate real equipment.

entries: Process preparation and parameter setup: Confirm material, datums, workholding, tools or dies, cutting parameters, and program versions against drawings and process sheets, then set tools and perform first-piece trial cutting.
Equipment operation and multiple-machine tending: Run more than one machine tool or robot simultaneously, load and unload to cycle times, adjust parameters, and maintain stable operation.
Process monitoring: Assess machining conditions through sound, vibration, temperature, chip form, pressure, and alarms, stopping promptly to handle abnormalities.

Dimensional and appearance verification: Use calipers, micrometers, gauges, or measuring tools to inspect critical dimensions, geometric tolerances, and surface quality against drawings, and determine acceptance, rework, or scrap.
Records and configuration control: Record batches, parameters, program versions, and inspection results, maintaining drawing, program, and process document versions through change procedures.

Maintenance and safety: Perform daily inspections and lubrication, remove chips and coolant, follow lockout/tagout, guarding, and personal protective equipment requirements, and report hazards immediately.

paragraphs: Multiple machine tool setters, operators, and tenders correspond to O*NET-SOC 51-4081.00. The official definition is to set up, operate, or tend more than one cutting or forming machine tool or robot. The scope excludes machinists primarily doing manual or single-machine work, tool and die makers primarily designing and making dies, and welding equipment operation roles centered on welding.

Work context (O*NET survey): 98% wear standard protective equipment daily; 95% have face-to-face discussions daily; 70% work in controlled indoor environments daily; 63% stand almost continually; 50% use their hands to handle or feel objects almost continually; and 61% work more than 40 hours weekly.

Work usually begins with process preparation: Check materials and batch quantities against drawings and process sheets, confirm datums and workholding, select tools or dies, import or call programs and set tools, then trial-cut and inspect the first piece. After acceptance, begin batch machining, load and unload to cycle times, and continuously monitor multiple machines.

Preparation and training: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zones 1—2 (SVP below 6.0), typically requiring a high school diploma or GED. Related experience ranges from little to several months, with on-the-job training from a few days to one year. The O*NET national training directory lists 315 related programs in machine tool and machining technology.

Key professional judgments: Interpret drawings and process requirements, identify dimensional and surface deviations, determine whether abnormalities arise from material, tools, workholding, or parameters, and decide whether to stop, adjust, change tools, or escalate. Leading O*NET work activities are obtaining information (86), identifying objects, actions, and events (85), controlling machines and processes (84), and inspecting equipment or materials (84).

Main outputs are parts meeting drawing and process requirements and batch records: Finished workpieces, first-piece and sampling inspection records, parameter and program version records, tool and measuring instrument replacement records, and abnormality and shutdown response records. Nonconforming products follow rework or scrap procedures.

Work cycle: Drawing and process sheet handover, workholding and parameter setup, first-piece trial cutting and inspection, batch machining and multiple-machine monitoring, scheduled sampling and dimensional judgments, abnormality shutdown and escalation, and batch and parameter record archiving. Every step is traceable and reviewable.

Machinists primarily perform manual and single-machine work, handling complete machining and fitting from drawing interpretation to finished products. Multiple machine tool operators tend more than one machine tool or robot simultaneously to produce batches at prescribed cycle times. Controlling the entire part's machining process and fitting differs from keeping multiple machines stable for batch output.

These comparisons draw on the O*NET O*NET-SOC 51-4081.00 definition, tasks, and adjacent occupation list, and BLS wage and employment definitions relayed by O*NET. Comparison dimensions are editorial syntheses, not official rankings or hiring standards.

First distinguish responsibility for an entire part's process from responsibility for stable multiple-machine operation and acceptable batches. Then compare adjacent directions' work objects, equipment scale, and responsibility boundaries, rather than equipment names alone.

Machinists usually complete drawing interpretation, workholding, machining, and fitting at single-machine or manual stations, taking responsibility for the entire part's process and fit. Multiple machine tool operators tend more than one machine tool or robot simultaneously, loading and unloading to process cycle times and monitoring conditions, with responsibility for batch stability and process records.

If you prefer exploring complete-part machining processes, fitting, and process improvement, compare machinists first. If you prefer stable multiple-machine operation to cycle times in batch production, controlling dimensional consistency and process records, this occupation is more direct.
Entry-level and current operators

First master checks against drawings and process documents, workholding and tool setting, measuring instrument use, and first-piece inspection. Gradually take on multiple-machine tending and parameter adjustment. Greater automation increases the need for people who can explain abnormalities and stop correctly.
Independent multiple-machine tenders

Treat automated scheduling, program and parameter management, tool-life data, and equipment condition data as supporting information. People still confirm first pieces, judge dimensions, handle material and tool abnormalities, and maintain records.
Programming and process roles
Use CAD/CAM and simulation to shorten programming and trial-cutting time while checking program versions, tool paths, and differences from actual machines, retaining traceable process change records.
Team leaders and quality staff

Analyze equipment condition and inspection data for trends, while responsible people still confirm batch release, nonconforming product disposition, and safety interlock management through procedures.

These reference different populations, not occupational percentiles.

US multiple machine tool operators (O*NET-SOC 51-4081.00) had 2025 median wages of US$22.68/hour and US$47,180/year. The median means half of workers earn above and half below this value. It is not entry-level pay, income after overtime, or a guaranteed wage at a particular factory.

For the same exact occupation, wages are US$35,780/year at the 10th percentile, US$39,420/year at the 25th, US$57,800/year at the 75th, and US$74,450/year at the 90th. The gap between the extremes generally reflects shifts, industry, region, skills, and tenure together. Lower percentiles cannot be labeled starting pay.

OEWS covers pretax pay for regular hours, including piecework, incentive pay, and production bonuses, while excluding overtime premiums and shift differentials. It is not total take-home income. Editorial suggestion: Check contractual pay methods, shifts, and overtime rules separately, without claiming night shifts in this occupation usually receive extra allowances.

When comparing roles, confirm pay method (hourly, piecework, or mixed), shifts and overtime rules, allowances and bonuses, whether protective equipment and training are provided, and whether measuring tools must be supplied personally. These terms can substantially affect actual income.
2025 industry shares: Manufacturing 80%, administrative support 11%, and others 9% (including wholesale). These are not industry wages or labor dispatch shares.

This page does not convert US figures into yuan, replace US occupational wages with Chinese industry averages, or use US wages to estimate Chinese income. The two markets have different statistical definitions and coverage.

entries: O*NET gives this occupation the interest code RC (Realistic, Conventional): a preference for hands-on equipment and tool operation and for following procedures and standards and maintaining records. Interests indicate only willingness to sustain these activities, not ability, hiring, or safety authorization.
Compare signals with specific machining tasks, supervisor feedback, and role requirements rather than interest scores alone.
One fit signal is steadiness and alertness: Maintaining attention through repetitive cycles and responding promptly to abnormal sounds, vibration, temperatures, and alarms.
Compare signals with actual multiple-machine tending performance, shutdown records, and supervisor feedback.

Another signal is following standards: Willingly checking drawings and process sheets item by item, accurately recording first-piece and sampling inspection results, and not skipping inspections based on experience.
Compare signals with inspection records, measuring instrument calibration records, and review feedback.

If you dislike repetitive cycles, prolonged standing, or strict safety and recordkeeping requirements, compare machinists, tool and die makers, or equipment repair roles. Automation levels vary by factory and affect the balance of physical work and monitoring.
Compare signals with real workshop rhythms rather than a single test result.

Do not screen yourself using MBTI, astrology, or one interest score. Start with paper process walkthroughs and measuring instrument reading exercises, then observe your actual response to repeated inspections, records, and abnormality handling.
Use assessments for exploration, not as a basis for hiring or authorization.

Hand-eye coordination and dimensional sensitivity can improve with practice. Drawing interpretation, measuring instrument use, parameter records, and abnormality escalation are also trainable behaviors observable through records.
Compare capability signals with reviewable machining and inspection records.

paragraphs: RC describes Realistic preferences for hands-on operation and Conventional preferences for procedural recordkeeping, not hiring, competence, or safety authorization. Extraversion or introversion cannot determine these alone.

Evidence level is exploratory: Interest codes and preparation levels come from the US O*NET occupational profile, without occupation-specific selection validity or adoption evidence. They cannot determine hiring, promotion, or safety authorization.

Boundaries: This editorially compiled checklist does not replace equipment manuals, process documents, employer safety procedures, or local laws. Specific protection, work permit, and lockout/tagout requirements follow on-site documents.

Editorial risk scenarios include entanglement/crushing from rotating or cutting equipment, chips and coolant, material handling, parameter errors, and abnormality responses. Check exposure against actual equipment; this occupation's Tasks do not directly establish an injection-molding specialization.

Evidence scope: Work-context percentages come from the O*NET work-context survey (US respondents, 26 items) and are not extrapolated to other regions. AI and automation boundaries reference O*NET tasks and technology signals and NIST AI RMF 1.0. Chinese wages use and identify the National Bureau of Statistics' 2025 manufacturing industry proxy.
Staff handling workholding, operation, loading and unloading, inspection, and handover for multiple cutting or forming machine tools.

Editorial risk analysis: Mechanical contact, splashes, exposure, and material handling require on-site assessment. No occupation-specific injury, occupational disease, or scrap rates were obtained. Work-context percentages are not health outcomes.

Boundaries: The entry route and capability ladder on this page are editorial explanations of control points that can be handled independently, not a uniform ranking or timetable. Specific requirements follow employers' and competent authorities' rules.
Can prepare workholding, obtain measuring tools, perform daily inspections and chip removal under supervision according to drawings and process sheets, and maintain accurate records.
Preparation and inspection assistance
Can independently set tools and parameters on one equipment type, trial-cut and inspect the first piece, sample at prescribed intervals, and determine acceptance or rework.
Independent single-machine operation
Can tend more than one machine tool or robot simultaneously, adjust parameters to cycle times, handle tool changes and material abnormalities, and maintain complete batch records.
Multiple-machine tending and parameter adjustment

Can make changeover and process adjustment judgments, review others' machining and inspection results, and participate in root-cause analysis of abnormalities and batch problems, without replacing quality inspection or safety management responsibilities.

ai_impact_table.responsibility_intro: The steps below describe the sequence of human controls when multiple machine tool operators use tools and automation features: input verification, conditions of use, output review, and recordkeeping.

responsibility_steps.说明: Check drawings, process sheets, program versions, material batches, and measuring instrument calibration status, confirming workholding and datums.
Start equipment only when guards are intact, interlocks effective, and programs and parameters confirmed. Do not bypass safety interlocks.
Have a person trial-cut and inspect first pieces, sample at prescribed intervals, and determine acceptance or rework. Do not release solely on system recommendations.
Record batches, parameters, program versions, tool changes, and inspection results to ensure traceability.
Stop, preserve evidence, and report through procedures when out-of-tolerance dimensions, abnormal sounds, alarms, or material abnormalities occur.

risk_rows.为什么重要: Causes batch scrap or tool and equipment damage
risk_rows.控制方式: Check program versions and process documents, verifying through first-piece trial cutting before batch production
Use guards and tools according to procedures, keeping hands away from moving components and cutting zones
Do not operate equipment with interlocks or guards bypassed. Stop and report abnormalities

risk_rows.为什么重要: Editorial risk scenario: Control splashes, sharp chips, and pooled fluids. No occupation-specific injury rates were obtained.
risk_rows.控制方式: Check isolation and shutdown conditions under equipment procedures before cleaning with dedicated tools. Select eye/skin protection for the exposure; do not broadly require gloves near accessible rotating components, because of entanglement risk.

risk_rows.为什么重要: Loading and unloading heavy workpieces can cause back and crushing injuries
risk_rows.控制方式: Use suitable lifting gear and fixtures and choose handling methods for the weight and space

risks.mitigation: Use guards and dedicated tools according to procedures, keeping hands away from cutting and forming areas while equipment runs
risks.scenario: Hands near moving components, cutting tools, or dies, or use of mismatched fixtures and tools
risks.title: Mechanical crushing and cutting risks

risks.consequence: Editorial risk scenario: Sharp chips, hot chips, splashes, and pooled fluids may cause contact hazards. No occupational incidence rates or respiratory effects were obtained.
risks.mitigation: For cleaning/maintenance, confirm shutdown, hazardous energy isolation, and safe conditions under procedures, and use dedicated cleaning tools. Select protection for the exposure, avoiding glove contact with rotating parts. | https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/216121
risks.scenario: Cleaning chips or replacing coolant without shutdown, or with guards left open
risks.title: Chip and coolant splash risks

risks.affected_roles: Staff setting parameters and selecting programs
risks.consequence: Batch scrap and tool and equipment damage
risks.mitigation: Check program versions and process documents, verify through first-piece trial cutting before batch production, and retain records
risks.scenario: Selecting the wrong program version, changing parameters without checks, or omitting first-piece verification
risks.title: Program or parameter error risks

risks.affected_roles: Staff working long term at machining stations
risks.consequence: Work context provides contaminant/noise signals but cannot establish causation or incidence of hearing damage or respiratory diseases.
risks.mitigation: Use on-site hazard assessments to determine noise/oil mist exposure, engineering controls, and applicable protection. O*NET's standard PPE percentage is not a configuration standard for specific protective equipment.
risks.scenario: Prolonged exposure to loud noise, oil mist, and dust with inadequate protection
risks.title: Noise and dust exposure risks

risks.affected_roles: Staff loading, unloading, and handling materials
risks.consequence: Tasks include positioning with lifting gear and material handling. No occupation-specific back/crushing injury rates were obtained. Assess weight, center of gravity, and isolation on site.
risks.mitigation: Select lifting gear and handling methods for the weight, work in pairs when needed, and keep routes clear
risks.scenario: Misjudging centers of gravity when loading, unloading, lifting, or moving heavy workpieces
risks.title: Material handling and lifting injury risks

risks.affected_roles: Staff running equipment and responding to abnormalities
risks.consequence: Personal injury and equipment damage, with missing records obscuring responsibility
risks.mitigation: Do not operate with interlocks or guards bypassed. Stop for abnormalities, preserve evidence, and report through procedures
risks.scenario: Bypassing interlocks to meet production targets, or failing to stop and report through procedures after alarms
risks.title: Safety interlock and abnormality response risks

components.definition_block: Multiple machine tool operators (51-4081.00) set up, operate, or tend more than one cutting or forming machine tool or robot to produce metal or plastic workpieces. Tasks include workholding, inspection, tool changes, lubrication, minor repairs, and supplemental CNC programming. Tasks may overlap with machinists and tool and die makers; judge by actual equipment and assigned responsibilities.

Use only fictional or public sample drawings and do not operate real equipment. Practice does not authorize equipment operation, special operations, or production safety responsibilities.

description.text: Multiple machine tool operators (O*NET-SOC 51-4081.00) set up, operate, or tend more than one cutting or forming machine tool or robot, including CNC, stamping, drilling and boring, turning, milling and planing, grinding, and welding equipment. This page compiles official O*NET tasks and work context, Job Zones 1—2 and high school diploma routes, the US 2025 BLS OEWS median annual wage of US$47,180 and -1% employment change for 2024—2034, mainland Chinese manufacturing industry proxy wages, AI and automation boundaries, fit signals, and entry routes.

subject.name: Multiple Machine Tool Setters, Operators, and Tenders
subject.summary: Multiple Machine Tool Setters, Operators, and Tenders, Metal and Plastic (O*NET-SOC 51-4081.00) set up, operate, or tend more than one cutting or forming machine tool or robot to machine and form metal and plastic parts. Work centers on workholding and parameter setup according to process documents, running and monitoring multiple machines, verifying dimensions and appearance against drawings, and records and abnormality escalation. This page uses official sources only to explain occupational scope, tasks, preparation requirements, and statistical definitions.
